9.0.0.en: These two verses are an introduction and presentation of the person of Saul the son of Kish. Since Saul was to become the first king of the children of Israel, it was fitting and proper to mention his lineage. Samuel tells us that he was the son of a Benjamite man named Kish the son of Abiel, and this man was known to be a mighty man of valor, that is, a man of influence and standing, in whom all the qualities of manhood were complete. As for Saul himself, he was a handsome young man, of splendid appearance, and there was none taller than he among all the people, that is, by physical standards he was the pride of all the youth of Israel. This is what the people asked for, physical standards and not spiritual standards, for they wanted a great appearance for the king in form and strength, and not his relationship with God and his piety.

9.1.0.en: Donkeys: the plural of she-donkey, the female of the donkey.

9.1.1.en: Kish, Saul's father, lost a group of donkeys that had perhaps been left grazing in the fields, and when he did not find them it was natural for him to assign his son, with one of the servants or workers of the house, to go and look for them.

9.2.0.en: Shalisha: it means three, and it is three small peaks of a mountain west of Ephraim, lying southwest of Shechem.

9.2.1.en: Saul was a young man equal to responsibility, for he covered a great distance in searching for the lost donkeys. He went north toward Ephraim, then west to the region of Shalisha, and he did not despair but went to another district called Shaalim.

9.3.0.en: The search for the donkeys continued, so they left Shaalim and headed to the land of "Zuph," near Ramah, where Samuel lived, and yet they found nothing. So Saul suggested returning to his father's house, for fear that the father's anxiety about the donkeys would turn to his son and he would send another to look for his son. A good quality in Saul appears here, namely his bearing of responsibility and his concern not to worry his parents, and this makes him worthy of kingship, though his pride corrupted his life and made him rejected by God.

9.3.1.en: We see here how God turns small events to carry out His will, for the loss of the donkeys was the means by which Saul met Samuel and Samuel anointed him king. So be confident that everything that passes in your life God uses for your good if you love Him.

9.4.0.en: The servant spoke with his master Saul and said to him: We are now beside the city of Ramah, where Samuel the man of God lives, and he is a man known to all the people as a prophet, and everything he says is from the Lord. So why do we not go to him and ask him, and he will guide us to the way and the place where we shall find the donkeys? The prophet is called "a man of God" because he leads his people in the way of God and prays for them before God. We should not wonder that Saul did not know the name of the prophet Samuel, for he lived in one of the villages and did not concern himself with general political affairs.

9.5.0.en: Saul did not object but accepted the servant's suggestion, but he wanted to honor the man of God and to give him a gift, yet he found no bread or anything that could be offered to him. The servant answered him that he had a fourth of a shekel of silver (equal to 3 grams of silver), and suggested offering it to the man of God, who would tell them about the way.

9.6.0.en: This verse is a parenthesis that interrupts the story of Saul and the donkeys, and the prophet Samuel mentioned it in his writing of this book to make clear two things:

9.6.1.en: The first: that people were accustomed to ask God through the man of God about everything that concerned them or was lost to them. The second: that the title prophet is a newer title that came into use in the last days of Samuel, in place of the common title for the prophet, which was "seer," that is, the one who sees the visions of God.

9.7.0.en: Saul approved of the servant's words and was reassured by the presence of the fourth of a shekel that he would offer to the prophet Samuel, and they went to Ramah to meet him.

9.8.0.en: Wells and watercourses were usually outside the cities, so while Saul and the servant were making their way up to the city of Ramah, they met the young women carrying jars to fill with water as they were coming down from high Ramah to the valley where the wells were. They asked them whether the seer was in the city.

9.9.0.en: The young women answered yes and asked Saul and the servant to hurry, because he had come today to Ramah and was also about to offer a sacrifice at the high place, that is, the altar that Samuel built in Ramah, his permanent residence (ch. 7:17).

9.10.0.en: The young women added that the people were gathered at the high place to offer the sacrifice and were waiting for Samuel to bless the sacrifice and then eat of it, so they could meet him on his way from his house to the high place.

9.11.0.en: Indeed they went up to the city, and as they headed toward its middle, they met Samuel coming out of his house on his way to the place of the sacrifice at the high place. Thus the loss of the donkeys made Saul seek Samuel to meet him, and from him he learned that God had chosen him as king, as you will see (vv. 15, 16). God allows everything to lead to our salvation if we love Him and submit to Him.

9.11.1.en: Take care to hear the voice of God in all the matters of your life through prayer and the guidance of the father of confession and spiritual guides, and your heart will be at ease and you will be strong in your steps, relying on God who supports you.

9.12.0.en: Had told Samuel in his ear: had revealed to Samuel.

9.12.1.en: In God's ordering and guiding of matters, just as He moved Saul because of the donkeys to meet Samuel, He also here prepares Samuel to receive Saul. The Lord revealed to Samuel, a day before Saul came to him, that tomorrow He would send him a Benjamite man to anoint as leader and king over Israel, and that He would enable him to save His people Israel from the humiliation of the Philistines, because He had heard the cry of His people and the time for deliverance had come. This does not contradict what is stated in (ch. 7:13), that the Philistines were defeated before the children of Israel and no longer attacked them, for the enmity was still present, as shown by their rising afterward and attacking the children of Israel. The people were crying out to God to give them a king who would always protect them from any Philistine attack or any enemies.

9.13.0.en: When Samuel went out on his way to the high place and saw Saul, the Lord spoke to him again and said to him: This is the man of whom I spoke to you, who will lead and restrain the people, that is, become king over them. At that moment Saul approached Samuel, not knowing who he was, and asked him where he could find the seer's house. We understand from this that Samuel was wearing ordinary clothes and had no large retinue around him, but was humble, walking quietly like the rest of the people. The expression "in the midst of the gate" means in the middle of the city gate, since all the ancient cities had gates that were closed at night to protect them.

9.14.0.en: Samuel answered Saul that he was the man Saul was seeking and looking for, and Samuel invited Saul and the servant accompanying him to go up with him to the high place, where Samuel would offer the sacrifice and then all would eat together. He also invited him to stay overnight until the morning of the next day, and he would tell him all that was on his mind. Of course God had already revealed all this to Samuel.

9.15.0.en: Samuel surprised Saul by telling him about the lost donkeys that they had been found. No one knew the story of the donkeys except Saul and the servant, so how did the man know this? Of course Samuel intended this to confirm to Saul that he was truly a man of God and knew his affairs, and this would be a greater motive for believing him in the important words he would say to him afterward. He let Saul know that he would obtain the greatest and finest thing in Israel, because he was to be king over it.

9.16.0.en: Saul did not understand Samuel's words or his hint, but was amazed at his speech and astonished at Samuel's knowledge of the story of the donkeys. At the same time he found the second part of his words incredible: how could all the wealth of Israel be his when he was a Benjamite, that is, of the tribe smallest in number and importance of all the tribes, and he and his family and his clan were also the least of the families in the tribe itself... With this Saul answered Samuel.

9.17.0.en: The parlor: a place like a hall beside the high place, set apart for eating the sacrifice.

9.17.1.en: After offering the sacrifice, Samuel took Saul and his servant and seated them with those invited in a special place called the parlor. The number of those invited as Samuel's guests was thirty men, and as a kind of honor Samuel seated Saul and his servant in the place of precedence before everyone.

9.18.0.en: It is understood implicitly from this verse that when Samuel slaughtered the sacrifice he took a part of it and gave it to the cook and charged him not to bring it out until he asked him for it, and here Samuel asked for it, so the cook brought the front leg with what was on it of meat and set it before Saul according to Samuel's command. It is known that the front leg was the priest's portion, and this means that Samuel gave his own portion to Saul and they ate together from it, which was a great honor from Samuel to Saul ... Samuel continued his speech saying that this was what was left of the whole sacrifice and that he had kept it for him as a portion, besides what was offered to all the people.

9.19.0.en: After the sacrifice and the feast were over, Samuel came down from the high place, taking Saul and the servant with him to his house, and went up with Saul to the roof of his house to speak with him. It is expected that he was preparing the matter for him, that he was to become king of Israel.

9.20.0.en: Saul spent the night on the roof of Samuel's house, and very early in the morning Samuel woke Saul to bid him farewell and send him to his father's house. After Saul woke up and he and Samuel came down and left the house, before reaching the city gate Samuel asked Saul to tell his accompanying servant to go ahead of them. Samuel's purpose in this was to be alone with Saul in order to let him hear the rest of God's decrees about his choice, and after this to anoint him king over Israel.

9.20.1.en: It is noted in the preceding verses that Samuel was preparing Saul to receive the news of his appointment as king from the time he met him at the gate until this verse, and then he will declare to him that he is the king at the beginning of the next chapter when he anoints him with oil. God in His love prepares a person for any great news, for He is considerate of the feelings of His children. May you take care of this in conveying news to others.

9.20.2.en: God honored Saul through Samuel and then made him king, but sadly he ruined his life by pride. May you thank God for His gifts and submit to His commandments with humility, and not forget your first weakness and helplessness and attribute God's gifts to yourself, thinking that you are great in yourself, so that God leaves you and you perish like Saul.

9.20.3.en: The anointing of Saul and his choice as king by lot

10.0.s.en: (1) The anointing of Saul as king

10.0.0.en: Flask: a small vessel in which oils or precious perfumes are placed.

10.0.1.en: The holy oil: it was oil that the priests used to anoint persons and holy things and consecrate them to God, and it was of pure olive oil with some perfumes added (Ex 30:22-25). Anointed you: anointing with oil was among the functions of the priest, and God appointed Samuel as priest in an exceptional manner because He refused that Eli and his offspring should be priests on account of their evils, and we find Samuel offering sacrifices in more than one place (ch. 9:12). Samuel, as prophet and priest, appointed by God in an exceptional manner, carried the flask of the anointing oil, and Saul, after Samuel's talks with him, was prepared for what was coming, so he lowered his head before Samuel, who in turn took from the oil of the flask and poured it on Saul's head as a sign of his anointing as king of Israel. Samuel added, saying that God is the One who anointed you over Israel (His inheritance) as king and leader, and then he kissed him as a sign of love from Samuel to the man chosen by God. Here appears Samuel's submission to the will of God in establishing the king, although the request from the people was wrong, for we find him welcoming the king and kissing him.

10.0.2.en: Beloved, in the grace and wealth of the New Testament, all of us were anointed with the anointing of the Holy Myron, so all of us became children of the King of heaven and earth, and we have a name in the book of life, and we have authority as kings over our senses and over all the power of the evil one; so do not forget what you received freely, and take care not to lose it, by submitting to the voice of God and keeping His commandments.

10.1.0.en: Rachel's tomb: it lies a mile north of Bethlehem and four miles from the southern border of Benjamin. Border: boundary.

10.1.1.en: Zelzah: it lies between Rachel's tomb and the southern border of Benjamin.

10.1.2.en: After Samuel anointed Saul king with the holy anointing oil, he began a prophetic discourse with him in which he told him of events that would happen, which God had revealed to Samuel. God's purpose in this was that Saul might be sure that his installation as king was from God directly, and that Samuel was truly the man of God. The first of these signs was that Saul, after Samuel left him, and before Saul left the border of the tribe of Benjamin, near Rachel's tomb at a place called Zelzah, would meet two men looking for him, who would tell him that his father had found the lost donkeys and that his father was concerned about nothing now except finding him.

10.1.3.en: By Samuel's words to Saul, Saul is assured that God, to whom he is consecrated and whose service he is to perform as king, will arrange all his affairs for him, however small they seem, like the loss of the donkeys, and that he must concentrate on the service of God.

10.2.0.en: Another prophetic sign Samuel gave Saul was that after that, at a place known to the Israelites having a large oak tree and called the "terebinth of Tabor," he would meet three men going up to "Bethel," which is a holy place to all the Israelites, since Jacob met God there and consecrated it, and this place afterward became a holy shrine for the Jews, who come and offer sacrifices in it. Of the three men, one is carrying three kids (young male goats), another three loaves of bread, and the third a skin of wine to pour out on the sacrifices that will be offered on the altar of "Bethel," and the men will give you two loaves for you and your servant to eat, so accept from them what they offered.

10.2.1.en: It is as if God also wanted to prove to Saul, the one chosen as king, that God is the One who provides for him and arranges his needs and feeds him in his hunger. This is a useful lesson he must not forget when he becomes king and receives the people's offerings in his honor, for it is God who gives to him through the people, so he will always know that God is the Giver and Provider.

10.2.2.en: The men did not give him a kid, because he is not a priest who offers sacrifices, nor to slaughter it and eat, lest he be occupied with the pleasures of food. For the same reason they did not give him wine, because it represents worldly joy, but gave him bread, which is the necessary sustenance with which he should be content, and not be occupied with the pleasures of the body but devote himself to the service of God and His people.

10.3.0.en: Gibeah: it means a high place or a hill, and there are several cities bearing the same name, and the Gibeah mentioned here is most likely Gibeah of Benjamin, lying about 6.5 km north of Jerusalem. The garrison of the Philistines: places where the camps and tents of the Philistines were pitched.

10.3.2.en: As for the third sign, you will continue on your way to the high place "Gibeah of God," which is so called because it is a place that some prophets chose to be in, and this place was also near the border of the Philistines, who had pitched their tents and camps there. At "Gibeah of God" you will meet a company of prophets coming down from the high place with their instruments of praise: a psaltery (the plural of lyre), a tabret (like a flute), a pipe and a harp. You will meet them as they praise God using their instruments.

10.4.0.en: And the Lord will give you a special gift, in that you will share with this company although you have no experience of what they do, and this will be a sign to you that God has given you a new heart and mind that were not yours, and you will become another man, different from what you knew in yourself.

10.4.1.en: Here appears the work of the Holy Spirit in the Old Testament, who would come temporarily upon the children of God to accomplish works. In the New Testament, however, He dwells permanently in the children of God after their Baptism through the sacrament of the Holy Myron.

10.4.2.en: Note: who are the prophets and the sons of the prophets: a spiritual group appeared from the days of the prophet Samuel and throughout the age of the monarchy of the people of the children of Israel. This group were disciples of a great prophet such as Samuel or Elijah or Elisha, and they had places where they gathered for the praise and glorification of the God of Israel. If their master, the great prophet, died, they followed the one after him or elected a leader for themselves from among themselves. They were not necessarily prophesying but praising, but this does not prevent some of them from being sent by God with certain prophecies to certain people, and the one of them who carried a prophecy and whose name was not declared was called "a man of God," as was said of the man who went and informed Eli the priest of his end.

10.5.0.en: Samuel continues his discourse with Saul and says: When these three signs that God gave you are fulfilled, you must be sure that God is with you and supports you in all your steps, so go and do what you see fit for the good of your people as their king.

10.6.0.en: Gilgal: a region beside Jericho, and it was a religious center in the days of Joshua.

10.6.1.en: Burnt offerings: sacrifices burned entirely to please God, and they are a symbol of the sacrifice of Christ on the Cross, which pleased God (Lev 1). Peace offerings: sacrifices offered to God of which the one offering eats with the priest, and they signify partaking of the Holy Mysteries (Lev 3). Before leaving him, Samuel asked Saul to go ahead of him to the region of Gilgal and wait for him there for a week, after which Samuel would come to him to offer to God burnt offerings and peace offerings in thanks to God for all that He had permitted and arranged for His people Israel and for the consecration of His servant Saul as their first king. There was another purpose in going to Gilgal, namely that Saul might spend a period of discipleship in which he would learn from Samuel. The importance of discipleship to spiritual fathers appears here.

10.6.2.en: It is noted that the Bible does not mention when Saul went to Gilgal, and most likely this took place after his victory over the Ammonites (ch. 11). Samuel's call to Saul to go to Gilgal was repeated afterward, as stated in (ch. 13:8).

10.6.3.en: Gilgal here reminds us of the monastery in which the priest spends a period of contemplation and learning before beginning service, which is a very important period in his life, and all of us are called to have periods of retreat to thank God, examine ourselves and review our goals and the way.

10.7.0.en: As soon as Samuel finished speaking with Saul and Saul turned to go on his way, we find that God gave him another heart and spirit. What is meant by the other heart is the resolve, seriousness and zeal that any person needs to accomplish his purposes. As for the signs that Samuel spoke of to Saul, they were all fulfilled as he prophesied and on the same day, and of course all this was to establish God's word in Saul's heart.

10.8.0.en: Prophesied: it does not necessarily mean that he spoke of future things, but prophesying also means prayer and praising God.

10.8.1.en: Saul and his servant arrived at Gibeah, as Samuel had said (v. 5), and indeed he met the prophets, and as another sign by which God wanted to distinguish Saul, the Holy Spirit came upon him, so he began to praise and glorify God exactly like the prophets, so that all the people who had known him for no short time and saw him prophesying were very amazed and said: What has happened to Saul the son of Kish? Has he also become a prophet from the company of the prophets?.!

10.9.0.en: And another said: Is not his father Kish, who is known to us, and they are all ordinary people, we have not heard that any of them prophesies ...!! Because of the strangeness of the matter it became a proverb in all Israel, which they say when something strange happens, for Saul was one of the young men far from God, and it was not expected of him that he would be among the prophets, and this was the proverb that came to be: "... Is Saul also among the prophets?"

10.9.1.en: There is another opinion about the phrase "who is their father": that what is meant is God, who is able to give the spirit of prophecy to any person He chooses. The third opinion is that what is meant is Samuel, the father of the school of the prophets, and he is a great prophet able to teach many, even those far away like Saul.

10.10.0.en: After Saul finished prophesying with the prophets, he came to the high place near Gibeah and met his uncle, who was anxious about him, he and the whole family, because of his absence for all this unexpected time in searching for the donkeys. The uncle asked him where he had been all this time, and he explained to him that the reason for his delay was his visit to Samuel to ask him about the place of the donkeys.

10.11.0.en: This aroused the curiosity of Saul's uncle, so he asked him what Samuel the man of God might have said, knowing of course this man's spirituality. But Saul did not tell all that Samuel had said, and cut his words very short, and mentioned only that Samuel told him that the donkeys had been found, while the rest of the matter he kept in his heart as his own secret.

10.11.1.en: In Saul's reply to his uncle many virtues are noticed, the most important of which are:

10.11.2.en: 1- His humility, for he did not show that he was the king.

10.11.3.en: 2- His wisdom, for he left the announcement of the matter of the kingdom to Samuel.

10.11.4.en: If the Holy Spirit came upon Saul and changed him and made him prophesy, He is also able to work in you, whatever your sins, to bring you to repentance, and even to bring you near to God so that you worship Him faithfully and praise Him, and then afterward you become one of His servants.

10.12.s.en: (3) The casting of lots to choose Saul as king

10.12.0.en: Samuel called the people together: this means the males over twenty years of age and not all the people, because these men represent all the families.

10.12.1.en: Mizpah: it lies about 13 km north of Jerusalem.

10.12.2.en: Samuel anointed Saul but did not declare anything to the people, so Samuel called the people and their leaders for this purpose, which was to announce Saul, the new king, to the people. Mizpah was the suitable place, as we pointed out before, because it is in a middle place among the lands of the tribes.

10.13.0.en: Samuel began his speech to the people by making clear that what he says is the word of the Lord and not his personal words. The Lord began His message to His people by reminding them of His great work of salvation and how He rescued them from the bondage of the Egyptians and from the kingdoms that stood in their way until they possessed the land.

10.14.0.en: Samuel pointed to the strange reaction of the people toward God: they rejected Him as king over them, though He is the only Savior who turned back their oppressors from them, and now they ask in place of Him for a king over them, and God agreed to that. Samuel made them stand before him according to the order of their tribes and the heads of their thousands (each tribe had a head over the thousand and a head over every fifty to judge and settle small disputes).

10.15.0.en: Samuel caused all the tribes to come near: this means that they all stood before God so that God might choose a tribe from them, and the most common method was casting lots with the names of all the tribes and choosing one name from them, and this is what was done, and the result of the divine lot fell to the tribe of Benjamin.

10.15.1.en: Although God had already chosen Saul and told Samuel so, Samuel did not announce this to the people for two reasons:

10.15.2.en: 1- Because some might doubt Samuel's word if he did not cast the lot.

10.15.3.en: 2- One of the tribes might be angry, especially those large in number or strength, if the king did not come from them.

10.16.0.en: After the tribe of Benjamin was chosen, all its clans came near, and from among the clans of the tribe the lot fell on the clan of Matri, in which was Saul, who was also chosen by lot from it. When the lot was declared and his name called, he did not appear, for he was hiding.

10.17.0.en: Those gathered were bewildered by Saul's disappearance, so they asked God through Samuel whether they would find him or not, and God answered them that Saul was there but was hidden among the baggage of the people who had come from their cities to Mizpah. Saul's hiding in this way was perhaps because of his sense of unworthiness, or fear of responsibility, or shyness at facing the people.

10.18.0.en: After God declared to them the place of Saul, some of the people ran to the baggage and brought him to the place of their gathering, and when he stood among them he was taller than all of them, so that the tallest man among the people did not reach above Saul's shoulder. Saul's distinction in physical terms appears here, and this is what the people asked for, but he was not distinguished spiritually, and it would have been more fitting for the people to ask for the wise, spiritual leader to lead them in the way of God.

10.19.0.en: Samuel presented Saul to the people, making clear that he was the Lord's choice for them, and that God had chosen the best of those who find approval with the people, and that it was not one in his appearance or the height of his stature. The people shouted, hailing Saul and expressing their joy that he had become king to them .. and "Long live the king" is the traditional cry among peoples for their kings, and its meaning is may God prolong the life of our king over us.

10.19.1.en: Of course God's choice of Saul was not His first divine desire, but He condescended and accepted the desire of His people, so He chose the best in the eyes of this people who rejected their heavenly King, so that the people might know the result of their choice according to material standards and not spiritual ones. The strange thing is that the people did not thank God for the new king, but were occupied with the gift rather than the Giver, that is, they were occupied with the king and forgot God.

10.20.0.en: After this Samuel began his speech with the people, explaining to them what the new monarchical system requires of rights and duties for the king, as well as the king's rights of the people's submission to him. We do not know the details of the speech of course, but he thought it good to write all that he said and put it in a book, which is considered the first civil constitution known to the people of Israel, defining the relationship between the king and the subjects. After Samuel finished his mission he sent the people and their leaders away, each to his house.

10.21.0.en: Saul also went away to his house, and many of his supporters followed him, whose hearts God had touched by His grace so that they loved Saul and followed him. But there were other people who despised Saul and belittled him and spoke against him with mocking words and did not bring him any gift, but Saul stopped his ears and did not hear their words. God and the holy inspired text described them as sons of Belial, an expression used for followers of Satan, or doers of evil, or those who worshipped idols.

10.21.1.en: Do not be disturbed if someone attacks you or directs criticism at you, but listen to him with humility, for it may be a message from God to you, and if you feel that the words are wrong and are enmity from the one speaking to you, then pray for him and do not enter into an unprofitable discussion with him.
